subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Peak Bias in Averages
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Peak Bias in Averages.

hook.text: A CEO earns $50 million. The company's 'average salary' is $200,000. Most workers earn $60,000.

buildup.text: The mean is pulled by extreme values. One outlier can distort the average beyond recognition.

discovery.text: We use averages as shortcuts, but they hide the shape of the distribution. Median tells a better story.

twist.text: Advertisers know this. 'Our average customer saves $500' hides that most save $50 and one saved $10,000.

climax.text: Whenever you hear 'average,' ask: mean or median? The gap between them reveals the hidden story.

punchline.text: Averages can lie without ever being wrong.

quiz.question: Why can averages be misleading?
options: Extreme values pull the mean away from the typical experience

details.summary: Peak bias in averages describes the tendency to judge a set of experiences by their peak moment rather than their average. A vacation with one amazing day is remembered more fondly than a uniformly pleasant vacation, because the peak dominates retrospective evaluation.
details.whyItMatters: Service design, product experience, and event planning benefit from understanding peak bias. Creating one extraordinary moment may generate more satisfaction than uniformly improving the entire experience. Memory is not a fair average of all moments.
takeaways: Peak moments dominate retrospective evaluation over consistent averages
One outstanding moment creates more positive memory than steady mediocrity
Experience designers should invest in creating memorable peaks rather than raising floor quality

faq.question: How does peak bias relate to the peak-end rule?
faq.answer: The peak-end rule states that experiences are judged primarily by their most intense moment and their ending. Peak bias is the broader principle that extreme moments dominate memory-based evaluation, overriding the actual average quality of the full experience.

faq.question: How can businesses apply peak bias to improve customer experience?
faq.answer: Instead of uniformly improving every touchpoint, invest disproportionately in creating one exceptional moment. A surprise upgrade, an unexpected gift, or an extraordinary interaction creates a memory peak that shapes overall satisfaction more than consistent adequacy.
